Some Of The Best Mods To Make It To Xbox One

I still think this is a terrible idea, not necessarily as a practice, but in how it's being executed.

Not because I'm some PCMR guy, but because I've modded enough games that I realize that troubleshooting is going to be a huge pain with console mods. Mods break stuff all the time, sometimes you don't find out until several hours into a game. That can be quite a while in something like Fallout where you can rack up a hundred hours plus of gameplay with a single playthrough.

With PC you can at least try to root out issues and fix them without having to wipe out the game or ruin hours of gameplay saves. This often means messing with game files and digging through the install folder and editing things manually. Something you can't do on consoles.

The lack of tools for troubleshooting isn't adequate and this is asking for all sorts of troubles in the future, especially considering a lot of mods are works in progress and update patches for both the mods themselves and the official developer patches and updates and will often break them.

PC gamers can often roll back updates or prevent them from installing to keep using mods that work with a particular version of the game. That is an option console gamers don't necessarily have.

I don't wish for console gamers to lose them, but the lack of any sort of system to address this is kind of problematic. I foresee a lot of frustrations in the future because of the closed operating system consoles run on, and the open system sometimes needed to troubleshoot and fix mod files.

People are going to pitch a fit the first time an update breaks a mod and makes it so the game won't launch when the modder has either stopped working on something, or takes a while to update it because modding isn't their job and they have other concerns.

Not to mention, just uninstalling a mod doesn't always work. It can invalidate a hundred hours worth of saves, and sometimes bits don't come out right and can screw up or break the game requiring either manually fixing it by rooting out the mod parts and replacing them, or a completely fresh install of a game. A PC gamer can back up a regular unmodded copy of a a game in case that happens, but console gamers can't do that as far as I know.

The only way this is going to work is if MS opens up the Xbox 1 file system some more to allow for troubleshooting, backing up game files, providing a way to prevent updates and roll back to previous versions, and provide more editing options for game files, or sooner or later things are going to get pretty messy.
